newsitem.title: USA: Chinese dissident wants to join Taiwan party.
newsitem.headline: Chinese dissident wants to join Taiwan party.

text.p: Chinese dissident Wang Xizhe, who recently fled China for the United States, said on Monday he would like to join Taiwan's Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang.

Speaking in public for the first time since leaving China, Wang said if the Chinese government could guarantee his safe return to China and if freedom of speech existed there, he would be willing to face Chinese charges that he illegally crossed the border into Hong Kong.

Wang told a news conference in Oakland, near San Francisco, that he would like to join the Kuomintang (KMT) in Taiwan. "My point is, this KMT is not just the KMT in Taiwan. In the eyes of the Chinese people of the mainland, KMT is a party all over China. I hope the KMT leadership will consider my membership application seriously," he said.

Wang, 46, one of China's leading dissidents, said through an interpreter he would not apply for political asylum in the United States until authorities in Taiwan gave him a definite answer on whether he could go there.

He fled to Hong Kong from his home in China's Guangdong province this month, just days after authorities in Beijing arrested pro-democracy activist Liu Xiaobo and ordered him to serve three years in a labour camp. The Chinese government has accused Wang of crossing the border illegally and has said Chinese authorities were pursuing those who helped him.
Wang and Liu recently wrote a letter demanding President Jiang Zemin be impeached for violating the constitution by placing the army under Communist Party, rather than state, control.

Wang said China was his homeland and naturally he would like to stay there, but he said persecution of pro-democracy activists had reached an unreasonable level. After Liu's arrest, he said he was under close surveillance.
Friends in the United States contacted him and asked him to consider leaving China, he said. "At that time, I told them I would not leave China until the last moment."

He said he decided to hide for a short time to decide what to do when he was contacted by a friend in Hong Kong, who also urged him to leave. Wang said he decided to leave after Hong Kong television reported he was missing.

Wang's activism dates from 1974 when he co-authored an attack in Guangdong on the radical 1966-76 Cultural Revolution. He took part in the 1979 Democracy Wall movement in Beijing and produced his own dissident newsletters.
He was twice imprisoned and spent 17 years in jail and labour camps. He was released on parole in 1993 and before he fled he had been under constant police surveillance.
Travelling via Europe, Wang arrived in the San Francisco Bay area last week.
